extracted.intended_audience: general readers and scholars of Benjamin Franklin's correspondence; readers interested in 18th-century political, moral, and editorial opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria, norms, and prescriptive statements found in a collection of Benjamin Franklin's late-18th-century letters (political, moral, editorial, and personal). These are guidance items and normative claims embedded in his correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settle international disputes by peaceful means/arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: “Discovery of a plan that would induce and oblige nations to settle their disputes without first cutting one another's throats.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin argues repeatedly that wars eventually become misfortunes even for the successful, and that mankind should be convinced to settle differences without fighting. He suggests arbitration (even by simple lot) as preferable to war: “Were they to do it even by the cast of a die, it would be better than by fighting and destroying each other.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper editors as guardians of national reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The conductor of a newspaper should, methinks, consider himself as in some degree the guardian of his country's reputation, and refuse to insert such writings as may hurt it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should decline to publish scandalous or personally abusive pieces that damage a country's reputation or needlessly distress distant subscribers; such abusive matter should, if printed at all, be confined to small pamphlets distributed by those who wish it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid printing personal abuse in general newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not fill newspapers with scandalous personal attacks and abusive writings that are 'so unprofitable and so disagreeable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin criticizes common newspaper practice of publishing personal abuse. He counsels that those who insist on printing abuses should do so in separate little pamphlets, not in general newspapers sent to wide audiences and subscribers in distant places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect civilians and civilian occupations in wartime
rubrics_metrics.description: In any future war certain descriptions of men should be undisturbed, have protection, and be permitted to follow their employments: 1. Cultivators of the earth; 2. Fishermen; 3. Merchants and traders in unarmed ships; 4. Artists and mechanics inhabiting and working in open towns. Hospitals should be unmolested and aided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a proposed improvement to the law of nations to reduce rapine and protect the peaceful, productive members of society. Franklin argues such protections would remove incentives for plunder and help make peace more lasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combatants only should be engaged; pay for requisitioned goods
rubrics_metrics.description: “In short, I would have nobody fought with but those who are paid for fighting... If obliged to take corn from the farmer, friend or enemy, I would pay him for it; the same for the fish or goods of the others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin proposes that limiting violence to paid soldiers and compensating civilians for taken goods reduces rewards of rapine, thereby diminishing encouragement for war and protecting innocents and producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relinquish privateering / oppose state-sanctioned plunder at sea
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate for the voluntary relinquishment of privateering and of plunder as an advantage of naval power, to avoid fostering piratical states and to protect commerce and peaceful merchants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin warns that privateering can create a taste for plunder and lead to corsair-like behavior; he urges leading naval powers to set an example by giving up the practice and thereby promoting secure mutual communications and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn duelling as irrational and murderous
rubrics_metrics.description: Duelling is 'murderous' and continues from absurd pride; it decides nothing and cannot justify death for petty affronts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin reasons historically and morally that duels no longer serve any fair decision-making purpose (unlike some older judicial uses) and thus are an unjustifiable practice that should be opposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic duty to pay taxes & public right to regulate property
rubrics_metrics.description: Money justly due from the people belongs to their creditors, and the public has rights to regulate descents, conveyances, and even to limit the quantity and uses of property; superfluous property may be disposed of by public laws for the public welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin frames taxation and property as social conventions: those who enjoy civil society must contribute (pay their debts/taxes), and the public legitimately regulates and reallocates property for the common good. Those who disagree may 'retire and live among savages.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Spend public resources on public utility rather than war
rubrics_metrics.description: The millions spent in wars could instead have produced public works—improved agriculture, navigable rivers, canals, bridges, aqueducts, roads, and other useful edifices—bringing great public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin uses this as an argument against war, showing concrete alternatives where war-expenditure would yield lasting improvements to society's comfort and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When evaluating or transcribing unwritten languages, account for interpreter orthography
rubrics_metrics.description: As the Indians had no letters, they had no orthography; Europeans learning an Indian language may each form their own orthography according to the usual powers of letters in their own tongue, so written forms can differ widely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and scholars should not assume different spellings denote different words; differences often reflect the transcriber's language conventions (English, French, German), and hyphenation or syllable markings were often omitted for technical/practical reasons (e.g., lack of hyphens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continue disagreeable engagements until they naturally terminate rather than rash separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice: 'for continuing to the end of the term, under all the present disagreeable circumstances: the connexion will then die a natural death.' Frequent changes are often made without amendment and often for the worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin illustrates with an anecdote (marshy meadow) to recommend patience and endurance in unpleasant situations because alternatives may be worse and time often resolves awkward relationships without public scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal frugality as a practical and enriching virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Frugality is an enriching virtue; Franklin praises frugal household management as valuable and sometimes economically advantageous in marriage and domestic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed in an anecdotal, prescriptive form: frugality may be personally beneficial and socially admirable, though Franklin admits he personally lacked it but benefited by finding it in a spouse.
